citations.quote: Let $H$ be a nonzero finite-dimensional complex inner-product space, and let $I_H:H\to H$ denote the identity map $x\mapsto x$. An **effect** on $H$ is an endomorphism $E$ such that both $E$ and $I_H-E$ are non-negative in the sense of [[def-non-negative-and-positive-operator]]. A **finite complete positive family** is a nonempty finite list $(E_1,\ldots,E_n)$ of non-negative endomorphisms with $\sum_{a=1}^n E_a=I_H$. The next lemma proves that every member of such a family is an effect, so the family is a finite complete effect family. This is algebraic data only; it does not assert a measurement law.

Let $V$ be a finite-dimensional real or complex inner product space and let
$T:V\to V$ be linear. The operator $T$ is **non-negative** when $T$ is
self-adjoint in the sense of [[def-self-adjoint-and-normal-endomorphism]] and

$$\langle Tv,v\rangle\ge 0$$

for every $v\in V$.

The operator $T$ is **positive** when $T$ is self-adjoint and

$$\langle Tv,v\rangle>0$$

for every nonzero $v\in V$.

derivations.claim: Fix $a\in\{1,\ldots,n\}$. The family identity gives $I_H-E_a=\sum_{b\ne a}E_b$. For every $x\in H$, each $\langle E_bx,x\rangle$ is a nonnegative real by [F2]; their finite sum is therefore nonnegative, including the empty sum $0$ when $n=1$. The sum is self-adjoint because each $E_b$ is self-adjoint and the sum is finite. Thus $I_H-E_a$ is non-negative.
Since $E_a$ is non-negative by [F1] and its complement is non-negative by step 1.1, it is an effect by the definition in [F1]. The index $a$ was arbitrary.

Let $H$ be a nonzero finite-dimensional complex inner-product space, with the root library's convention that the inner product is linear in its first argument. A **density operator** on $H$ is a non-negative endomorphism $\rho:H\to H$ with $\operatorname{tr}(\rho)=1$; non-negative and trace have the meanings of [[def-non-negative-and-positive-operator]] and [[def-trace-of-an-endomorphism]]. The zero-dimensional space is excluded: its only endomorphism has trace $0$.

Here $\ker\rho=\{x\in H:\rho x=0\}$, using the kernel of a linear map from [[def-kernel-and-image-of-a-linear-map]]. The **support** of $\rho$ is the orthogonal complement of its kernel in the root convention:

$$\operatorname{supp}(\rho):=\{x\in H: \langle x,y\rangle=0\text{ for every }y\in\ker\rho\}.$$

For a subspace $S\subseteq H$, $\rho$ is **faithful on $S$** when $\operatorname{supp}(\rho)=S$ and the restriction $\rho|_S:S\to S$ is positive definite in the sense of [[def-non-negative-and-positive-operator]]. This restriction is an endomorphism: if $x\in S$ and $y\in\ker\rho$, self-adjointness gives $\langle\rho x,y\rangle=\langle x,\rho y\rangle=0$, so $\rho x\in(\ker\rho)^\perp=S$.

Let $V$ be a finite-dimensional real or complex inner product space and let
$T:V\to V$ be linear. The operator $T$ is **non-negative** when $T$ is
self-adjoint in the sense of [[def-self-adjoint-and-normal-endomorphism]] and

$$\langle Tv,v\rangle\ge 0$$

for every $v\in V$.

The operator $T$ is **positive** when $T$ is self-adjoint and

$$\langle Tv,v\rangle>0$$

for every nonzero $v\in V$.

Let $\mathbb F$ be $\mathbb R$ or $\mathbb C$, with **conjugation** $z\mapsto\overline z$
the identity on $\mathbb R$ and complex conjugation on $\mathbb C$
([[def-complex-conjugate-real-imaginary-part-and-modulus]]). A **real** or
**complex inner-product space** is an $\mathbb F$-vector space $V$ together with
an inner product $\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle:V\times V\to\mathbb F$ in the sense
of [[def-inner-product-space]]: for all $u,v,w\in V$ and $a,b\in\mathbb F$,

$$\langle au+bv,w\rangle=a\langle u,w\rangle+b\langle v,w\rangle,\qquad \langle u,v\rangle=\overline{\langle v,u\rangle},\qquad \langle v,v\rangle\ge0,\quad \langle v,v\rangle=0\iff v=0 .$$

**Conjugate-linearity in the second argument.** Conjugate symmetry together with
linearity in the first argument gives, for all $w\in V$,

$$\langle w,au+bv\rangle=\overline{\langle au+bv,w\rangle}=\overline{a\langle u,w\rangle+b\langle v,w\rangle}=\overline a\,\langle w,u\rangle+\overline b\,\langle w,v\rangle .$$

**Induced length.** The **induced length**, or inner-product norm, of $v$ is

$$\|v\|:=\sqrt{\langle v,v\rangle},$$

which is exactly the published [[def-inner-product-norm]]: positive definiteness
makes $\langle v,v\rangle$ a nonnegative real with a unique nonnegative square
root, so that $\|v\|\ge0$, $\|v\|=0$ exactly for $v=0$, and
$\langle v,v\rangle=\|v\|^2$.

**The convention on this page.** Every inner-product space below is real or
complex in this sense, the pairing is linear in the first argument and
conjugate-linear in the second, and $\|v\|$ always denotes the induced length.
In the real case conjugation is the identity and $|z|$ is the absolute value of
$\mathbb R$; in the complex case they are complex conjugation and the complex
modulus. All statements below are therefore written once and read in either
scalar field.

Let $V$ be a finite-dimensional vector space over $F$ and let $T:V\to V$ be
linear. Choose any ordered basis $\mathcal B$ of $V$ and define the **trace of
the endomorphism $T$** by

$$\operatorname{tr}(T):=\operatorname{tr}([T]_{\mathcal B}^{\mathcal B}).$$

This is independent of the chosen basis: matrices of the same endomorphism in
two ordered bases are similar, and similar matrices have equal trace. When
$V$ is the zero space, the empty basis gives trace $0$.

For a square matrix $A=(a_{ij})\in M_n(F)$, its **trace** is the sum of its
diagonal entries,

$$\operatorname{tr}(A):=\sum_{i\in n}a_{ii}.$$

For $n=0$, this is the empty sum, so the unique empty matrix has trace $0$.

For every natural $n$, the map
$\operatorname{tr}:M_n(F)\to F$ is linear:

$$\operatorname{tr}(A+B)=\operatorname{tr}(A)+\operatorname{tr}(B),\qquad \operatorname{tr}(\lambda A)=\lambda\operatorname{tr}(A).$$

Let $V$ be a vector space over a field $F$ ([[def-vector-space]]).

$V$ is **finite-dimensional over $F$** when it has a **finite** basis
([[def-linear-basis]], [[def-countable]]): some basis $B$ of $V$ satisfies
$B \approx n$ for some $n \in \mathbb{N}$ ([[def-equinumerous]]).

For such a $V$, the **dimension of $V$ over $F$**, written $\dim_F V$, is that
$n$:

$$\dim_F V \;:=\; \text{the unique } n \in \mathbb{N} \text{ such that } V \text{ has a basis } B \text{ with } B \approx n .$$

**This is well defined.** Existence of such an $n$ is the hypothesis, together
with the fact that a finite set is equinumerous with exactly one natural number
([[lem-pigeonhole]], claim 3). Uniqueness is
[[thm-any-two-finite-bases-have-the-same-size]]: two bases of $V$ with $n$ and
with $m$ elements force $n = m$. That theorem is therefore a **prerequisite** of
this definition, not a later justification of it, and it is listed in `deps`.

$V$ is **infinite-dimensional over $F$** when it is not finite-dimensional over
$F$, that is, when $V$ has **no** finite basis. No number is attached to such a
space here: the symbol $\dim_F V$ is defined only in the finite-dimensional case,
and the expression $\dim_F V = \infty$ is not used.

**The zero space.** $\varnothing$ is a basis of $\{0_V\}$
([[def-linear-basis]]) and $\varnothing \approx 0$, so $\{0_V\}$ is
finite-dimensional with $\dim_F \{0_V\} = 0$. Conversely a space of dimension $0$
has a basis $B \approx 0$, that is $B = \varnothing$, and then
$V = \operatorname{span}(\varnothing) = \{0_V\}$
([[def-linear-combination-and-span]]).

derivations.claim: Put $\rho=I_H/d$. The scalar $1/d$ is positive real. The identity is self-adjoint, and for every $x\in H$, $\langle\rho x,x\rangle=(1/d)\langle x,x\rangle\ge0$ by [F3] and [F7]. Thus $\rho$ is non-negative by [F2].
In a basis of $H$ with $d$ elements, the matrix of $\rho$ is $(1/d)I_d$. By [F4]–[F6], its trace is $(1/d)\sum_{j=1}^d1=1$. Therefore $\rho$ is a density operator by [F1].

citations.quote: Let $H$ be a nonzero finite-dimensional complex inner-product space. Two nonzero vectors $x,y\in H$ represent the same **ray** when $y=\alpha x$ for some nonzero $\alpha\in\mathbb C$. A **pure state** is such a ray. If $u$ is a unit representative, its associated operator is $P_u=|u\rangle\langle u|$, with the bra, ket and outer-product convention of [[def-qc-dirac-notation-conversion]]. The theorem [[thm-qc-ray-projector-well-defined-and-bijective]] proves that this operator is a rank-one orthogonal projection independent of the chosen unit representative, so it is the operator representative of the pure state.

All complex inner products in this track use the root convention: they are
linear in the first argument and conjugate-linear in the second
([[def-real-and-complex-inner-product-space]]). For vectors $x,y$ in the same
space, define the Dirac pairing by

$$\langle x|y\rangle_D:=\langle y,x\rangle_{\mathrm{root}}.$$

The ket $|x\rangle$ denotes the vector $x$. The bra $\langle x|$ denotes the
linear functional $z\mapsto\langle z,x\rangle_{\mathrm{root}}$.

For finite-dimensional complex inner-product spaces $H,K$, vectors $y\in H$ and
$x\in K$, define the rank-one linear map

$$|x\rangle\langle y|:H\to K,\qquad z\mapsto\langle z,y\rangle_{H,\mathrm{root}}x.$$

Given ordered orthonormal bases of $H$ and $K$, its coordinate matrix is
$[x][y]^\dagger$, where $[x]$ and $[y]$ are the corresponding coordinate
columns and $M^\dagger:=\overline M^{\mathsf T}$ is the conjugate transpose.
The coordinate assertion is established in
[[thm-qc-dirac-notation-coordinate-identity]].

Let $W$ be a subspace of a finite-dimensional inner product space $V$. The orthogonal-decomposition theorem ([[thm-finite-dimensional-orthogonal-decomposition]]) gives

$$V=W\oplus W^\perp$$

and associates to every $v\in V$ unique vectors $w\in W$ and $z\in W^\perp$ with $v=w+z$. The **orthogonal projection onto $W$** is the function

$$P_W:V\longrightarrow W,\qquad P_Wv=w.$$

Equivalently, $P_Wv$ is the unique vector of $W$ such that $v-P_Wv\in W^\perp$.

Let $V$ be a finite-dimensional real or complex inner product space and let
$T:V\to V$ be linear. The operator $T$ is **non-negative** when $T$ is
self-adjoint in the sense of [[def-self-adjoint-and-normal-endomorphism]] and

$$\langle Tv,v\rangle\ge 0$$

for every $v\in V$.

The operator $T$ is **positive** when $T$ is self-adjoint and

$$\langle Tv,v\rangle>0$$

for every nonzero $v\in V$.

Let $V$ be a finite-dimensional vector space over $F$ and let $T:V\to V$ be
linear. Choose any ordered basis $\mathcal B$ of $V$ and define the **trace of
the endomorphism $T$** by

$$\operatorname{tr}(T):=\operatorname{tr}([T]_{\mathcal B}^{\mathcal B}).$$

This is independent of the chosen basis: matrices of the same endomorphism in
two ordered bases are similar, and similar matrices have equal trace. When
$V$ is the zero space, the empty basis gives trace $0$.

For a square matrix $A=(a_{ij})\in M_n(F)$, its **trace** is the sum of its
diagonal entries,

$$\operatorname{tr}(A):=\sum_{i\in n}a_{ii}.$$

For $n=0$, this is the empty sum, so the unique empty matrix has trace $0$.
Every finite-dimensional real or complex inner product space has an orthonormal basis. In dimension zero, this is the empty basis.

Let $T:V\to W$ be a linear map whose domain $V$ is finite-dimensional over
$F$. Its **nullity** and **rank** are

$$\operatorname{nullity}T:=\dim_F(\ker T),\qquad \operatorname{rank}T:=\dim_F(\operatorname{im}T).$$

Both dimensions are defined. The kernel is a linear subspace of the
finite-dimensional space $V$, so it is finite-dimensional by
[[thm-linear-kernel-image-and-injectivity]] and
[[thm-dimension-of-a-linear-subspace]]. The image is finite-dimensional because
[[lem-kernel-basis-extension-gives-image-basis]] constructs a finite basis of
it from a basis of $V$. Thus rank and nullity are natural numbers, including
when $V$ is the zero space.

derivations.claim: Let $u$ be unit and suppose $v=\alpha u$ is another unit representative of the same ray. Then $1=\|v\|^2=|\alpha|^2\|u\|^2$, so $|\alpha|=1$. By [F2], $P_vz=\langle z,\alpha u\rangle\alpha u=\overline\alpha\alpha\langle z,u\rangle u=P_uz$ for every $z$. Thus the projector does not depend on the unit representative.

By [F2], $P_u^2z=\langle z,u\rangle\langle u,u\rangle u=P_uz$. Its range is $\mathbb C u$, a one-dimensional subspace, so [F7] gives rank one. For every $z$, $P_uz\in\mathbb C u$ and $$\langle z-P_uz,u\rangle=\langle z,u\rangle-\langle z,u\rangle\langle u,u\rangle=0,$$ so the residual is in $(\mathbb C u)^\perp$; by the residual characterization in [F3], $P_u$ is the orthogonal projection onto $\mathbb C u$. Also, for all $z,w$, $\langle P_uz,w\rangle=\langle z,u\rangle\langle u,w\rangle=\langle z,P_uw\rangle$ and $\langle P_uz,z\rangle=|\langle z,u\rangle|^2\ge0$. Hence $P_u$ is non-negative by [F4]. Choose an orthonormal basis $(e_j)$ by [F6] and write $u=\sum_jc_je_j$; then $\langle P_ue_j,e_j\rangle=|c_j|^2$, so [F5] gives $\operatorname{tr}(P_u)=\sum_j|c_j|^2=\langle u,u\rangle=1$ by orthonormality.

Conversely, let $P$ be a rank-one orthogonal projection onto $W$. By [F7], $\dim W=1$, so choose a unit $u\in W$. For every $z$, write $Pz=\alpha u$; [F3] gives $z-Pz\in W^\perp$, so $\langle z,u\rangle=\langle Pz,u\rangle=\alpha$. Therefore $Pz=\langle z,u\rangle u=P_uz$, proving surjectivity. If $P_u=P_v$, their ranges are equal, so $u$ and $v$ span the same line and represent the same ray. This proves injectivity and the claimed bijection.

An **ordered tensor register** consists of a finite ordered list of
finite-dimensional complex inner-product spaces $H_0,\ldots,H_{n-1}$, each
equipped with a specified ordered orthonormal basis. Its space is
$H_0\otimes\cdots\otimes H_{n-1}$, with factors retained in the displayed
order. The product basis is ordered lexicographically by its tuple of factor
indices. The empty tensor product is $\mathbb C$ with basis $\{1\}$. A
zero-dimensional factor is allowed in this mathematical construction and makes
the tensor space zero; it is not a register under
[[def-qc-register-and-computational-basis]].

The inner product is linear in the first argument and conjugate-linear in the
second, and on elementary tensors it is

$$\left\langle\bigotimes_{k<n}x_k,\bigotimes_{k<n}y_k\right\rangle_{\otimes}:=\prod_{k<n}\langle x_k,y_k\rangle_{{\rm root},k}.$$ 

For the empty tensor, the right side is the empty product $1$, giving the
standard inner product on $\mathbb C$.

For a permutation $\sigma$ of the $n$ factor positions, the **wire permutation**
$P_\sigma$ maps the product basis vector indexed by
$(i_0,\ldots,i_{n-1})$ to the product basis vector whose output factor order is
$(\sigma(0),\ldots,\sigma(n-1))$. It is extended linearly; for $n=0$ it is the
identity on $\mathbb C$. The extension is a linear map in the sense of
[[def-linear-map]].

All complex inner products in this track use the root convention: they are
linear in the first argument and conjugate-linear in the second
([[def-real-and-complex-inner-product-space]]). For vectors $x,y$ in the same
space, define the Dirac pairing by

$$\langle x|y\rangle_D:=\langle y,x\rangle_{\mathrm{root}}.$$

The ket $|x\rangle$ denotes the vector $x$. The bra $\langle x|$ denotes the
linear functional $z\mapsto\langle z,x\rangle_{\mathrm{root}}$.

$$|x\rangle\langle y|:H\to K,\qquad z\mapsto\langle z,y\rangle_{H,\mathrm{root}}x.$$

Given ordered orthonormal bases of $H$ and $K$, its coordinate matrix is

columns and $M^\dagger:=\overline M^{\mathsf T}$ is the conjugate transpose.

Let $T:V\to W$ be a linear map between finite-dimensional real or complex inner
product spaces, and let $r$ be the number of positive singular values of $T$.
Then there exist orthonormal bases $(e_1,\dots,e_n)$ of $V$ and
$(f_1,\dots,f_m)$ of $W$, together with singular values

$$s_1\ge\cdots\ge s_r>0,$$

such that

$$Tv=\sum_{j=1}^r s_j\langle v,e_j\rangle f_j$$

for every $v\in V$.
Every finite-dimensional real or complex inner product space has an orthonormal basis. In dimension zero, this is the empty basis.

For $x,y\in\mathbb R^n$ and $z,w\in\mathbb C^n$, the formulas

$$\langle x,y\rangle_{\mathbb R^n}=\sum_{k<n}x_ky_k,\qquad \langle z,w\rangle_{\mathbb C^n}=\sum_{k<n}z_k\overline{w_k}$$

define inner products, linear in the first argument. At $n=0$, the unique pairing on the zero space is an inner product.

Define the complex-linear map $T_C:\mathbb C^n\to\mathbb C^m$ by $(T_Cz)_i=\sum_{k=1}^n c_{ik}z_k$; its standard matrix is exactly $C$. Apply the positive-family construction [F3] to $T_C$. If $q_j$ and $p_j$ are its right and positive left singular vectors, the identity there gives $T_Cz=\sum_{j=1}^r s_j\langle z,q_j\rangle p_j$. Evaluating at each standard basis vector of $\mathbb C^n$ and using [F5], the $(i,k)$ entry of this identity is $c_{ik}=\sum_{j=1}^r s_j(p_j)_i\overline{(q_j)_k}$. This is the coefficient formula needed below, obtained from the positive singular families without a codomain basis completion.

Define $u_j=\sum_i(p_j)_ie_i$ and $v_j=\sum_k\overline{(q_j)_k}f_k$. The coordinate columns of the $p_j$ are orthonormal by [F3]–[F5], so the $u_j$ are orthonormal. For the second family, $\langle v_j,v_\ell\rangle=\sum_k\overline{(q_j)_k}(q_\ell)_k=\overline{\langle q_j,q_\ell\rangle}=\delta_{j\ell}$, so it too is orthonormal. The coefficient of $e_i\otimes f_k$ in $\sum_js_ju_j\otimes v_j$ is $\sum_js_j(p_j)_i\overline{(q_j)_k}=c_{ik}$ by step 1.1, so this sum equals $\Psi$. If $C=0$, then $\Psi=0$ and $r=0$. The positive coefficients are precisely the positive singular values of $C$.

By [F1], the vectors $u_j\otimes v_j$ are orthonormal: their pairings are $\langle u_i,u_j\rangle\langle v_i,v_j\rangle=\delta_{ij}$. Expanding the squared norm of the sum in step 2.1 therefore gives $\|\Psi\|^2=\sum_js_j^2$, including the empty sum when $\Psi=0$.

Let $V$ be a vector space over a field $F$ ([[def-vector-space]]).

### Finite sums of vectors

By axiom (V1) the triple $(V, +, 0_V)$ is an abelian group ([[def-group]]), hence
in particular a commutative monoid ([[def-semigroup-and-monoid]]). So the finite
products of [[def-monoid-finite-product]] are available in it, and we write them
**additively**: for $n \in \mathbb{N}$ and a finite list $u : n \to V$, that is a
function on the von Neumann natural $n = \{0, \dots, n-1\}$
([[def-natural-numbers]], [[lem-nat-order-is-membership]]),

$$\sum_{i<n} u_i \;:=\; \prod_{i<n} u_i \quad \text{computed in } (V,+,0_V),$$

so that $\sum_{i<0} u_i = 0_V$ and $\sum_{i<\sigma(n)} u_i = \bigl(\sum_{i<n} u_i\bigr) + u_n$,
and the value depends only on $u_0, \dots, u_{n-1}$.

### Linear combinations

A **linear combination in $V$** is a vector of the form

$$\sum_{i<n} \lambda_i v_i$$

where $n \in \mathbb{N}$, $\lambda : n \to F$ is a finite list of scalars and
$v : n \to V$ is a finite list of vectors; the sum is the finite sum just
described, of the list $i \mapsto \lambda_i v_i$. For $S \subseteq V$, a vector
$w \in V$ is a **linear combination of elements of $S$** when there are
$n \in \mathbb{N}$, $\lambda : n \to F$ and $v : n \to S$ with
$w = \sum_{i<n} \lambda_i v_i$.

**The empty case is a real case.** $\mathbb{N}$ contains $0$
([[def-natural-numbers]]), and at $n = 0$ the sum is the empty sum, which is
$0_V$. So $0_V$ is a linear combination of elements of every subset of $V$,
including $S = \varnothing$. The lists are indexed from $0$, so a linear
combination of length $n$ is $\lambda_0 v_0 + \dots + \lambda_{n-1}v_{n-1}$; no
statement here is restricted to $n \ge 1$.

### The span

Let $S \subseteq V$. The set of linear subspaces of $V$ containing $S$ is
nonempty, since $V$ itself is one, so its intersection is a linear subspace of
$V$ by [[lem-intersection-of-linear-subspaces]]. That intersection is the **span
of $S$**,

$$\operatorname{span}(S) \;:=\; \bigcap \{\, W \;:\; W \text{ is a linear subspace of } V \text{ and } S \subseteq W \,\} .$$

It contains $S$, being an intersection of sets each of which contains $S$, and it
is contained in every linear subspace of $V$ that contains $S$. So it is the
**smallest** linear subspace of $V$ containing $S$, and those two properties
determine it uniquely: if $W$ and $W'$ both contain $S$ and are each contained in
every linear subspace containing $S$, then each is contained in the other. This
is what licenses the definite article.

A subset $S \subseteq V$ **spans** $V$, or is a **spanning set** of $V$, when
$\operatorname{span}(S) = V$.

For a linear subspace $W$ ([[def-linear-subspace]]) of an inner product space $V$, using the preceding notion of orthogonality ([[def-orthogonal-vectors-sets-and-orthonormal-bases]]), its **orthogonal complement** is

$$W^\perp:=\{v\in V:\langle v,w\rangle=0\text{ for every }w\in W\}.$$

This is a linear subspace: $0\in W^\perp$, and linearity in the first argument shows that $au+bv\in W^\perp$ whenever $u,v\in W^\perp$ and $a,b$ are scalars. One has $V^\perp=\{0\}$ by positive definiteness and $\{0\}^\perp=V$.

If $W$ is a subspace of a finite-dimensional real or complex inner product space $V$, then

$$V=W\oplus W^\perp.$$

Thus every $v\in V$ has unique vectors $w\in W$ and $z\in W^\perp$ with $v=w+z$.

proper linear subspace of an infinite-dimensional space whose basis is
equinumerous with a basis of the whole space.
Every finite-dimensional real or complex inner product space has an orthonormal basis. In dimension zero, this is the empty basis.

Let $H,K$ be finite-dimensional complex inner-product spaces with ordered
orthonormal bases $E=(e_j)_{j<n}$ and $F=(f_i)_{i<m}$. Let $T:H\to K$ be
linear ([[def-linear-map]]), and write $T_{ij}$ for the $(i,j)$ entry of its
matrix in these bases.
Then, for every $z\in H$,

$$Tz=\sum_{j<n}\sum_{i<m}T_{ij}\langle z,e_j\rangle_{H,\mathrm{root}}f_i, \qquad T=\sum_{j<n}\sum_{i<m}T_{ij}|f_i\rangle\langle e_j|.$$

For $x\in K$ and $y\in H$, the rank-one map $|x\rangle\langle y|$ has
coordinate matrix $[x]_F[y]_E^\dagger$, where $M^\dagger=\overline M^{\mathsf T}$.
Its amplitude satisfies
$\langle x|T|y\rangle_D=\langle Ty,x\rangle_{K,\mathrm{root}}$.
All sums are empty when an index dimension is zero, and the identities include
those cases.

Let $H_0,\ldots,H_{n-1}$ be a finite ordered list of finite-dimensional
complex inner-product spaces with specified ordered orthonormal bases of
sizes $d_0,\ldots,d_{n-1}$, allowing $d_k=0$. The elementary tensors of the
factor bases, ordered lexicographically, form an orthonormal basis of the
tensor register, and

$$\dim(H_0\otimes\cdots\otimes H_{n-1})=\prod_{k<n}d_k.$$

For the empty list the product is $1$ and the tensor space is $\mathbb C$; if
any $d_k=0$, the tensor space is zero and the product basis is empty.

Let $\mathcal B=(b_0,\ldots,b_{n-1})$ be an ordered basis of $V$. The unique
coordinates $v=\sum_{j<n}x_jb_j$ form the **coordinate column**
$[v]_{\mathcal B}\in M_{n\times1}(F)$, whose $j$-th entry is $x_j$.

Let $\mathcal C=(c_0,\ldots,c_{m-1})$ be an ordered basis of $W$ and let
$T:V\to W$ be linear. The **matrix of $T$ relative to $\mathcal B$ and
$\mathcal C$** is the matrix
$[T]_{\mathcal B}^{\mathcal C}\in M_{m\times n}(F)$ whose $j$-th column is
$[T(b_j)]_{\mathcal C}$. Equivalently, if
$T(b_j)=\sum_{i<m}t_{ij}c_i$, then
$([T]_{\mathcal B}^{\mathcal C})_{ij}=t_{ij}$.

For an empty ordered basis, these definitions give the unique coordinate column
or matrix of the corresponding zero-sized shape.

Let $F$ be a field, let $m,n,p\in\mathbb N$, and let
$A=(a_{ij})\in M_{m\times n}(F)$ and
$B=(b_{jk})\in M_{n\times p}(F)$. Their **matrix product** is the matrix
$AB\in M_{m\times p}(F)$ whose entries are

$$(AB)_{ik}:=\sum_{j\in n}a_{ij}b_{jk}.$$

The sum is the finite sum in the additive commutative monoid of $F$. If $n=0$,
it is the empty sum, so $AB$ is the zero matrix of shape $m$ by $p$.

The **identity matrix** $I_n\in M_n(F)$ has entry $1$ when $i=j$ and entry $0$
when $i\ne j$. In particular, $I_0$ is the unique empty matrix in $M_0(F)$.

For $A=(a_{ij})\in M_{m\times n}(F)$, the **transpose** of $A$ is the matrix
$A^{\mathsf T}\in M_{n\times m}(F)$ defined by

$$(A^{\mathsf T})_{ji}:=a_{ij}.$$

Thus transposition interchanges rows and columns. The transpose of a zero-sized
matrix is the unique matrix of the transposed zero-sized shape.

Every $z\in\mathbb C$ has unique coordinates $z=a+bi$
([[thm-complex-numbers-form-a-field]]). Define
$$\operatorname{Re}z=a,\qquad \operatorname{Im}z=b,\qquad \overline z=a-bi,$$
and define its **modulus** by
$$|z|=\sqrt{a^2+b^2}.$$
The real numbers are least-upper-bound complete
([[cor-cauchy-reals-lub-complete]]), so the nonnegative square root exists and
is unique by [[thm-of-square-roots]].

For a linear map $T:V\to W$, its **kernel** and **image** are respectively

$$\ker T:=\{v\in V:T(v)=0_W\},\qquad \operatorname{im}T:=\{T(v):v\in V\}.$$

That both sets are linear subspaces, and that a trivial kernel characterises
injectivity, is proved in [[thm-linear-kernel-image-and-injectivity]].

derivations.claim: By [F1]–[F2], the barycenter $\rho$ is a density operator, as required for the purification hypothesis. By [F3], write $\Psi=\sum_{j=1}^r\sqrt{\lambda_j}\,e_j\otimes f_j$ with $\lambda_j>0$ and orthonormal families; $r\ge1$ because $\Psi$ is a unit vector. Set $S=\operatorname{span}\{e_1,\ldots,e_r\}$ and $L=\operatorname{span}\{f_1,\ldots,f_r\}$. By [F13]–[F14], the complements $S^\perp$ and $L^\perp$ are finite-dimensional and have orthonormal bases; adjoining those bases completes the Schmidt families to orthonormal bases of $H$ and $K$. The basis-independent partial-trace formula [F5]–[F6], together with [F7], gives $\rho=\operatorname{Tr}_K(|\Psi\rangle\langle\Psi|)=\sum_j\lambda_j|e_j\rangle\langle e_j|$. This operator is positive with eigenvalue $\lambda_j$ on $e_j$ and zero on $S^\perp$; the orthogonal decomposition shows $\ker\rho=S^\perp$, so the support definition [F9] and kernel definition [F18] give $S=\operatorname{supp}(\rho)$. The expansion of $\Psi$ shows that its auxiliary support is $L$.

If $p_a>0$ and $x\in\ker\rho$ as defined in [F18], then $0=\langle\rho x,x\rangle=\sum_bp_b\langle\sigma_bx,x\rangle$. Every summand is nonnegative by [F9], so $\langle\sigma_ax,x\rangle=0$. Writing $R_a=\sqrt{\sigma_a}$ by [F10], self-adjointness gives $\langle\sigma_ax,x\rangle=\langle R_ax,R_ax\rangle=0$, hence $\sigma_ax=0$. Self-adjointness then gives $\langle\sigma_ay,x\rangle=0$ for every $y$, so $\sigma_a y\in S$.

On $S$, define $R e_j=\lambda_j^{-1/2}e_j$ and $A_a=p_aR(\sigma_a|_S)R$ when $p_a>0$; put $A_a=0$ when $p_a=0$. Each $A_a$ is self-adjoint because $R$ and $\sigma_a|_S$ are self-adjoint, and it is non-negative because its quadratic form is $p_a\langle\sigma_aRx,Rx\rangle\ge0$. Since $\sum_ap_a\sigma_a=\rho$, one has $\sum_aA_a=R(\rho|_S)R=I_S$.

By [F13], $K=L\oplus L^\perp$; choose an orthonormal basis of $L^\perp$ by [F14], so $(f_j)$ together with that basis is an orthonormal basis of $K$. On $L$, define $E_a$ by the matrix $A_a^T$ in $(f_j)$ and extend it by zero on $L^\perp$. Since each $A_a$ is self-adjoint, $A_a^T$ is self-adjoint; for every coordinate vector $z$, [F17] gives $z^*A_a^Tz=\overline{(\bar z)^*A_a\bar z}\ge0$, so this block is non-negative. Their sum is identity on $L$ and zero on $L^\perp$. Choose $a_0$ with $p_{a_0}>0$, which exists since $\sum_ap_a=1$, and add the projection $0\oplus I_{L^\perp}$ to $E_{a_0}$. The resulting operators are non-negative and sum to $I_K$, so [F11]–[F12] make them a complete effect family. In particular, $E_a=0$ when $p_a=0$.

Let $\Lambda e_j=\sqrt{\lambda_j}e_j$ and $S_a=\sqrt{E_a}$. Each $E_a$ is block diagonal on $L\oplus L^\perp$. The direct sum of the non-negative square roots of its two blocks is a non-negative square root of $E_a$, so uniqueness in [F10] shows that $S_a$ is block diagonal. If $B_a$ is the matrix of $S_a|_L$ in $(f_j)$, then $B_a$ is self-adjoint and $B_a^2=A_a^T$.

Put $T_a=I_H\otimes S_a$ and $\Phi_a=T_a\Psi$. On elementary tensors, [F4], [F8] and self-adjointness of $S_a$ give $\langle T_a(x\otimes y),x'\otimes y'\rangle=\langle x\otimes y,T_a(x'\otimes y')\rangle$; since elementary tensors span by [F16], $T_a$ is self-adjoint. By [F7], for every $z$, $T_a|\Psi\rangle\langle\Psi|T_a z=\langle T_a z,\Psi\rangle T_a\Psi=\langle z,T_a\Psi\rangle\Phi_a=|\Phi_a\rangle\langle\Phi_a|z$. Thus the displayed filtered operator is the outer product of $\Phi_a$. In the ordered Schmidt product basis, $\Psi$ has coefficient matrix $\Lambda$, and [F8] sends $e_i\otimes f_j$ to $e_i\otimes S_af_j$; row-by-column multiplication [F17] gives coefficient matrix $C_a=\Lambda B_a^T$ on $H\otimes L$.

By [F5], [F7], [F15]–[F17], the partial trace of the filtered vector's outer product has matrix $C_aC_a^*=\Lambda B_a^T\overline{B_a}\Lambda$. Since $B_a$ is self-adjoint, $B_a^T=\overline{B_a}$; hence $B_a^T\overline{B_a}=\overline{B_a^2}=\overline{A_a^T}=A_a$, the last equality using self-adjointness of $A_a$. Therefore the reduced operator on $S$ is $\Lambda A_a\Lambda=p_a\sigma_a|_S$, by the definition of $A_a$ and $\Lambda R=I_S$.

If $p_a>0$, step 1.2 shows that $\sigma_a$ vanishes on $S^\perp$, so the operator identity from step 6.1 extends to all of $H$. If $p_a=0$, step 3.1 gives $E_a=0$, so the filtered vector and $p_a\sigma_a$ are both zero. This proves the required identity for every outcome.

citations.quote:
Let $\rho$ be a density operator on a nonzero finite-dimensional complex-inner-product space $H$. Then there are $m=\operatorname{rank}(\rho)\ge1$, positive numbers $\lambda_1,\ldots,\lambda_m$ with $\sum_{j=1}^m\lambda_j=1$, and orthonormal unit vectors $e_1,\ldots,e_m$ such that

$$\rho=\sum_{j=1}^m\lambda_j|e_j\rangle\langle e_j|.$$

The eigenvectors with eigenvalue zero are omitted; the displayed pure-state projectors are pairwise orthogonal.

Let $H$ be a nonzero finite-dimensional complex-inner-product space. A **finite ensemble of density operators** on $H$ is a positive integer $n$, weights $p_1,\ldots,p_n\ge0$ with $\sum_{a=1}^np_a=1$, and density operators $\rho_1,\ldots,\rho_n$ on $H$. Its **barycenter** is $\bar\rho=\sum_{a=1}^np_a\rho_a$. A zero-weight component still names a density operator but contributes zero to the barycenter.

Let $K$ be any finite-dimensional complex-inner-product space. A **purification** of a density operator $\rho$ on $H$ is a unit vector $\Psi\in H\otimes K$ such that

$$\operatorname{Tr}_K(|\Psi\rangle\langle\Psi|)=\rho.$$

The tensor factors are ordered $H$ then $K$. Tensor products, outer products and partial trace have the conventions of [[def-qc-tensor-register-and-permutation]], [[def-qc-dirac-notation-conversion]] and [[def-qc-partial-trace]]. The auxiliary space may be any finite dimension that supports such a unit vector.

Let $H,K$ be finite-dimensional complex-inner-product spaces with the tensor-product convention of [[def-qc-tensor-register-and-permutation]]. For every $\Psi\in H\otimes K$ there are an integer $r\ge0$, positive numbers $s_1,\ldots,s_r$, and orthonormal families $u_1,\ldots,u_r\in H$ and $v_1,\ldots,v_r\in K$ such that

$$\Psi=\sum_{j=1}^r s_j u_j\otimes v_j,\qquad \|\Psi\|^2=\sum_{j=1}^r s_j^2.$$

For $\Psi=0$ take $r=0$ and the empty sum. For any chosen ordered pair of orthonormal bases, the construction below obtains the $s_j$ as the positive singular values of the coefficient matrix of $\Psi$ in their ordered product basis.

An **ordered tensor register** consists of a finite ordered list of
finite-dimensional complex inner-product spaces $H_0,\ldots,H_{n-1}$, each
equipped with a specified ordered orthonormal basis. Its space is
$H_0\otimes\cdots\otimes H_{n-1}$, with factors retained in the displayed
order. The product basis is ordered lexicographically by its tuple of factor
indices. The empty tensor product is $\mathbb C$ with basis $\{1\}$. A
zero-dimensional factor is allowed in this mathematical construction and makes
the tensor space zero; it is not a register under
[[def-qc-register-and-computational-basis]].

The inner product is linear in the first argument and conjugate-linear in the
second, and on elementary tensors it is

$$\left\langle\bigotimes_{k<n}x_k,\bigotimes_{k<n}y_k\right\rangle_{\otimes}:=\prod_{k<n}\langle x_k,y_k\rangle_{{\rm root},k}.$$ 

For the empty tensor, the right side is the empty product $1$, giving the
standard inner product on $\mathbb C$.

For a permutation $\sigma$ of the $n$ factor positions, the **wire permutation**
$P_\sigma$ maps the product basis vector indexed by
$(i_0,\ldots,i_{n-1})$ to the product basis vector whose output factor order is
$(\sigma(0),\ldots,\sigma(n-1))$. It is extended linearly; for $n=0$ it is the
identity on $\mathbb C$. The extension is a linear map in the sense of
[[def-linear-map]].

For a finite ordered family of finite-dimensional complex vector spaces
$H_k,K_k$ and complex-linear maps $T_k:H_k\to K_k$, the **tensor map**
$\bigotimes_{k<n}T_k:H_0\otimes\cdots\otimes H_{n-1}\to
K_0\otimes\cdots\otimes K_{n-1}$ is the unique linear map satisfying

$$\left(\bigotimes_{k<n}T_k\right)(x_0\otimes\cdots\otimes x_{n-1})=T_0x_0\otimes\cdots\otimes T_{n-1}x_{n-1}.$$

For $n=0$, the tensor map is the identity map $z\mapsto z$ on the empty tensor
product $\mathbb C$.

All complex inner products in this track use the root convention: they are
linear in the first argument and conjugate-linear in the second
([[def-real-and-complex-inner-product-space]]). For vectors $x,y$ in the same
space, define the Dirac pairing by

$$\langle x|y\rangle_D:=\langle y,x\rangle_{\mathrm{root}}.$$

The ket $|x\rangle$ denotes the vector $x$. The bra $\langle x|$ denotes the
linear functional $z\mapsto\langle z,x\rangle_{\mathrm{root}}$.

For finite-dimensional complex inner-product spaces $H,K$, vectors $y\in H$ and
$x\in K$, define the rank-one linear map

$$|x\rangle\langle y|:H\to K,\qquad z\mapsto\langle z,y\rangle_{H,\mathrm{root}}x.$$

Given ordered orthonormal bases of $H$ and $K$, its coordinate matrix is
$[x][y]^\dagger$, where $[x]$ and $[y]$ are the corresponding coordinate
columns and $M^\dagger:=\overline M^{\mathsf T}$ is the conjugate transpose.
The coordinate assertion is established in
[[thm-qc-dirac-notation-coordinate-identity]].

For a complex vector space $H$, write $\operatorname{End}(H)$ for the set of
linear maps $H\to H$ ([[def-linear-map]]).

Let $H_A,H_B$ be finite-dimensional complex inner-product spaces with fixed
ordered orthonormal bases $(e_i)_{i<a}$ and $(f_j)_{j<b}$, respectively. The
ordered product basis of $H_A\otimes H_B$ has the $A$ index first. For
$R\in\operatorname{End}(H_A\otimes H_B)$ define
$\operatorname{Tr}_B(R)\in\operatorname{End}(H_A)$ by

$$\bigl(\operatorname{Tr}_B(R)\bigr)_{i i'}:=\sum_{j<b}R_{(i,j),(i',j)}.$$

Rows are output coordinates and columns are input coordinates, as in
[[def-coordinate-column-and-matrix-of-a-linear-map]]. If $b=0$, the sum is
empty and equals $0$. The notation $\operatorname{Tr}_B$ means that the second
factor is contracted; the first factor and its order are retained.

Let $V$ be a vector space over a field $F$ ([[def-vector-space]]).

### Finite sums of vectors

By axiom (V1) the triple $(V, +, 0_V)$ is an abelian group ([[def-group]]), hence
in particular a commutative monoid ([[def-semigroup-and-monoid]]). So the finite
products of [[def-monoid-finite-product]] are available in it, and we write them
**additively**: for $n \in \mathbb{N}$ and a finite list $u : n \to V$, that is a
function on the von Neumann natural $n = \{0, \dots, n-1\}$
([[def-natural-numbers]], [[lem-nat-order-is-membership]]),

$$\sum_{i<n} u_i \;:=\; \prod_{i<n} u_i \quad \text{computed in } (V,+,0_V),$$

so that $\sum_{i<0} u_i = 0_V$ and $\sum_{i<\sigma(n)} u_i = \bigl(\sum_{i<n} u_i\bigr) + u_n$,
and the value depends only on $u_0, \dots, u_{n-1}$.

### Linear combinations

A **linear combination in $V$** is a vector of the form

$$\sum_{i<n} \lambda_i v_i$$

where $n \in \mathbb{N}$, $\lambda : n \to F$ is a finite list of scalars and
$v : n \to V$ is a finite list of vectors; the sum is the finite sum just
described, of the list $i \mapsto \lambda_i v_i$. For $S \subseteq V$, a vector
$w \in V$ is a **linear combination of elements of $S$** when there are
$n \in \mathbb{N}$, $\lambda : n \to F$ and $v : n \to S$ with
$w = \sum_{i<n} \lambda_i v_i$.

**The empty case is a real case.** $\mathbb{N}$ contains $0$
([[def-natural-numbers]]), and at $n = 0$ the sum is the empty sum, which is
$0_V$. So $0_V$ is a linear combination of elements of every subset of $V$,
including $S = \varnothing$. The lists are indexed from $0$, so a linear
combination of length $n$ is $\lambda_0 v_0 + \dots + \lambda_{n-1}v_{n-1}$; no
statement here is restricted to $n \ge 1$.

### The span

Let $S \subseteq V$. The set of linear subspaces of $V$ containing $S$ is
nonempty, since $V$ itself is one, so its intersection is a linear subspace of
$V$ by [[lem-intersection-of-linear-subspaces]]. That intersection is the **span
of $S$**,

$$\operatorname{span}(S) \;:=\; \bigcap \{\, W \;:\; W \text{ is a linear subspace of } V \text{ and } S \subseteq W \,\} .$$

It contains $S$, being an intersection of sets each of which contains $S$, and it
is contained in every linear subspace of $V$ that contains $S$. So it is the
**smallest** linear subspace of $V$ containing $S$, and those two properties
determine it uniquely: if $W$ and $W'$ both contain $S$ and are each contained in
every linear subspace containing $S$, then each is contained in the other. This
is what licenses the definite article.

A subset $S \subseteq V$ **spans** $V$, or is a **spanning set** of $V$, when
$\operatorname{span}(S) = V$.

For a linear subspace $W$ ([[def-linear-subspace]]) of an inner product space $V$, using the preceding notion of orthogonality ([[def-orthogonal-vectors-sets-and-orthonormal-bases]]), its **orthogonal complement** is

$$W^\perp:=\{v\in V:\langle v,w\rangle=0\text{ for every }w\in W\}.$$

This is a linear subspace: $0\in W^\perp$, and linearity in the first argument shows that $au+bv\in W^\perp$ whenever $u,v\in W^\perp$ and $a,b$ are scalars. One has $V^\perp=\{0\}$ by positive definiteness and $\{0\}^\perp=V$.

If $W$ is a subspace of a finite-dimensional real or complex inner product space $V$, then

$$V=W\oplus W^\perp.$$

Thus every $v\in V$ has unique vectors $w\in W$ and $z\in W^\perp$ with $v=w+z$.

Let $V$ be a vector space over a field $F$ ([[def-vector-space]]) that is
finite-dimensional with $\dim_F V = n$ ([[def-dimension]]), and let $U$ be a
linear subspace of $V$ ([[def-linear-subspace]]). Then

1. $U$ is finite-dimensional over $F$ and $\dim_F U \le n$;
2. $\dim_F U = n$ **if and only if** $U = V$;
3. **Extension, with no choice principle.** Every linearly independent
   $A_0 \subseteq U$ is contained in a basis of $U$: there is a basis $B$ of $U$
   with $A_0 \subseteq B \subseteq U$. Claim 1 is the case $A_0 = \varnothing$.
   Since $V$ is itself a linear subspace of $V$ ([[def-linear-subspace]]), claim 3
   applies with $V$ in place of $U$, and hence to **any** finite-dimensional
   vector space over $F$ in place of the pair $(V, U)$.

**Nothing above uses a choice principle**, and claim 3 in particular is the
finite-dimensional substitute for the Zorn-based extension theorem stated earlier
on this page. In finite dimension the extension terminates on its own, because
[[cor-independent-set-is-no-larger-than-a-finite-spanning-set]] bounds the size
of an independent set and [[thm-well-ordering-principle]] then supplies a largest
one; no selection is made anywhere.

**Finiteness is essential in claim 2.** Without it the equality case fails: the
companion page exhibits a
proper linear subspace of an infinite-dimensional space whose basis is
equinumerous with a basis of the whole space.
Every finite-dimensional real or complex inner product space has an orthonormal basis. In dimension zero, this is the empty basis.

For finite-dimensional complex inner-product spaces $H_A,H_B$, the partial
trace $\operatorname{Tr}_B:\operatorname{End}(H_A\otimes H_B)\to
\operatorname{End}(H_A)$ is the unique linear map satisfying

$$\operatorname{tr}\bigl((\operatorname{Tr}_B R)\circ T\bigr)=\operatorname{tr}\bigl(R\circ(T\otimes I_{H_B})\bigr)\quad\text{for every }R\in\operatorname{End}(H_A\otimes H_B)\text{ and }T\in\operatorname{End}(H_A).$$

Here $I_{H_B}$ is the identity map $y\mapsto y$ on $H_B$; $\operatorname{End}$
is the notation defined in [[def-qc-partial-trace]].

Its coordinate formula is independent of the chosen ordered orthonormal basis
of $H_B$. The assertion includes zero-dimensional factors.

Let $F$ be a field ([[def-field]]), let $n \in \mathbb{N}$, let $V$ be a vector
space over $F$ ([[def-vector-space]]) and let $U$ be a family of linear subspaces
$U_i$ of $V$ indexed by $i < n$ ([[def-linear-subspace]],
[[def-sum-of-linear-subspaces]]) with

$$V \;=\; \bigoplus_{i<n} U_i$$

([[def-internal-direct-sum]]) and every $U_i$ finite-dimensional over $F$
([[def-dimension]]). Then $V$ is finite-dimensional over $F$ and

$$\dim_F V \;=\; \sum_{i<n} \dim_F U_i ,$$

the right-hand side being the finite sum of [[def-monoid-finite-product]] read
additively in the commutative monoid $(\mathbb{N}, +, 0)$
([[def-nat-addition]], [[lem-nat-add-identity]],
[[lem-nat-add-associative]], [[lem-nat-add-commutative]]).

**The base case is a genuine case.** At $n = 0$ the direct sum of the empty
family is $\{0_V\}$ and the empty sum of natural numbers is $0$, so the formula
reads $\dim_F\{0_V\} = 0$. **At $n = 2$** it reads
$\dim_F(U \oplus W) = \dim_F U + \dim_F W$.

**No choice principle is used.** The only inputs are
[[thm-dimension-formula]] and [[thm-dimension-of-a-linear-subspace]], both of
which are proved in finite dimension without one.

Let $F$ be a field ([[def-field]]), let $n \in \mathbb{N}$ and let $F^{n}$ be the
function space on the von Neumann natural $n = \{0, \dots, n-1\}$, with the
pointwise operations ([[def-function-space]], [[def-natural-numbers]],
[[lem-nat-order-is-membership]]). For $i < n$ define the **standard unit vector**
$e_i \in F^{n}$ by

$$e_i(i) = 1_F, \qquad e_i(j) = 0_F \ \text{ for } j < n \text{ with } j \ne i .$$

Then:

1. **Finite sums in a function space are pointwise.** For every set $X$, every
   $p \in \mathbb{N}$, every list $u : p \to F^{X}$ and every $j \in X$,
   $$\Bigl(\sum_{k<p} u_k\Bigr)(j) \;=\; \sum_{k<p} u_k(j),$$
   the right-hand sum being taken in $(F,+,0_F)$. (Stated here for an arbitrary
   $X$ because the companion page needs it at $X = \mathbb{N}$.)
2. $e : n \to F^{n}$ is an ordered basis of $F^{n}$ ([[def-linear-basis]]); in
   particular $e$ is injective and its image $e[n] = \{\, e_i : i < n \,\}$ is a
   basis of $F^{n}$ with $e[n] \approx n$ ([[def-equinumerous]]);
3. for every $\lambda : n \to F$ and every $j < n$,
   $\bigl(\sum_{i<n}\lambda_i e_i\bigr)(j) = \lambda_j$; equivalently the
   coordinate list of $x \in F^{n}$ with respect to the ordered basis $e$
   ([[thm-unique-coordinates-with-respect-to-an-ordered-basis]]) is
   $i \mapsto x(i)$;
4. $F^{n}$ is finite-dimensional over $F$ with $\dim_F F^{n} = n$
   ([[def-dimension]]);

The theorem [[thm-qc-ray-projector-well-defined-and-bijective]] proves that this operator is a rank-one orthogonal projection independent of the chosen unit representative, so it is the operator representative of the pure state.

Let $H$ be a nonzero finite-dimensional complex inner-product space, with the root library's convention that the inner product is linear in its first argument. A **density operator** on $H$ is a non-negative endomorphism $\rho:H\to H$ with $\operatorname{tr}(\rho)=1$; non-negative and trace have the meanings of [[def-non-negative-and-positive-operator]] and [[def-trace-of-an-endomorphism]]. The zero-dimensional space is excluded: its only endomorphism has trace $0$.

Here $\ker\rho=\{x\in H:\rho x=0\}$, using the kernel of a linear map from [[def-kernel-and-image-of-a-linear-map]]. The **support** of $\rho$ is the orthogonal complement of its kernel in the root convention:

$$\operatorname{supp}(\rho):=\{x\in H: \langle x,y\rangle=0\text{ for every }y\in\ker\rho\}.$$

For a subspace $S\subseteq H$, $\rho$ is **faithful on $S$** when $\operatorname{supp}(\rho)=S$ and the restriction $\rho|_S:S\to S$ is positive definite in the sense of [[def-non-negative-and-positive-operator]]. This restriction is an endomorphism: if $x\in S$ and $y\in\ker\rho$, self-adjointness gives $\langle\rho x,y\rangle=\langle x,\rho y\rangle=0$, so $\rho x\in(\ker\rho)^\perp=S$.

For nonzero finite-dimensional complex-inner-product $H$, the map sending a ray $[u]$ to the rank-one projector $P_u=|u\rangle\langle u|$ of any unit representative is well-defined and bijective onto the rank-one orthogonal projections on $H$. Each $P_u$ is non-negative and has trace one.

$$\rho=\sum_{j=1}^m\lambda_j|e_j\rangle\langle e_j|.$$

$$\operatorname{tr}(T):=\operatorname{tr}([T]_{\mathcal B}^{\mathcal B}).$$

$$\operatorname{tr}(A+B)=\operatorname{tr}(A)+\operatorname{tr}(B),\qquad \operatorname{tr}(\lambda A)=\lambda\operatorname{tr}(A).$$

Let $K$ be any finite-dimensional complex-inner-product space. A **purification** of a density operator $\rho$ on $H$ is a unit vector $\Psi\in H\otimes K$ such that

$$\operatorname{Tr}_K(|\Psi\rangle\langle\Psi|)=\rho.$$

The tensor factors are ordered $H$ then $K$. Tensor products, outer products and partial trace have the conventions of [[def-qc-tensor-register-and-permutation]], [[def-qc-dirac-notation-conversion]] and [[def-qc-partial-trace]]. The auxiliary space may be any finite dimension that supports such a unit vector.

Let $H,K$ be finite-dimensional complex-inner-product spaces with the tensor-product convention of [[def-qc-tensor-register-and-permutation]]. For every $\Psi\in H\otimes K$ there are an integer $r\ge0$, positive numbers $s_1,\ldots,s_r$, and orthonormal families $u_1,\ldots,u_r\in H$ and $v_1,\ldots,v_r\in K$ such that

$$\Psi=\sum_{j=1}^r s_j u_j\otimes v_j,\qquad \|\Psi\|^2=\sum_{j=1}^r s_j^2.$$

For $\Psi=0$ take $r=0$ and the empty sum. For any chosen ordered pair of orthonormal bases, the construction below obtains the $s_j$ as the positive singular values of the coefficient matrix of $\Psi$ in their ordered product basis.

Every density operator $\rho$ on a nonzero finite-dimensional complex-inner-product space $H$ has a purification on some finite-dimensional auxiliary space. More precisely, if $r=\operatorname{rank}(\rho)$, it has one on an auxiliary space of dimension $r$. If $\Psi_i\in H\otimes K_i$ ($i=1,2$) are any two purifications of the same $\rho$, then for every integer $m\ge\max(\dim K_1,\dim K_2)$ and every pair of linear isometric embeddings $\iota_i:K_i\to\mathbb C^m$, where $\mathbb C^m$ has its standard complex inner product, there is a unitary $U$ on $\mathbb C^m$ such that

$$ (I_H\otimes U)(I_H\otimes\iota_2)\Psi_2=(I_H\otimes\iota_1)\Psi_1. $$

An **ordered tensor register** consists of a finite ordered list of
finite-dimensional complex inner-product spaces $H_0,\ldots,H_{n-1}$, each
equipped with a specified ordered orthonormal basis. Its space is
$H_0\otimes\cdots\otimes H_{n-1}$, with factors retained in the displayed
order. The product basis is ordered lexicographically by its tuple of factor
indices. The empty tensor product is $\mathbb C$ with basis $\{1\}$. A
zero-dimensional factor is allowed in this mathematical construction and makes
the tensor space zero; it is not a register under
[[def-qc-register-and-computational-basis]].

The inner product is linear in the first argument and conjugate-linear in the
second, and on elementary tensors it is

$$\left\langle\bigotimes_{k<n}x_k,\bigotimes_{k<n}y_k\right\rangle_{\otimes}:=\prod_{k<n}\langle x_k,y_k\rangle_{{\rm root},k}.$$ 

For the empty tensor, the right side is the empty product $1$, giving the
standard inner product on $\mathbb C$.

For a permutation $\sigma$ of the $n$ factor positions, the **wire permutation**

identity on $\mathbb C$. The extension is a linear map in the sense of
[[def-linear-map]].

linear in the first argument and conjugate-linear in the second
([[def-real-and-complex-inner-product-space]]). For vectors $x,y$ in the same
space, define the Dirac pairing by

$$\langle x|y\rangle_D:=\langle y,x\rangle_{\mathrm{root}}.$$

The ket $|x\rangle$ denotes the vector $x$. The bra $\langle x|$ denotes the
linear functional $z\mapsto\langle z,x\rangle_{\mathrm{root}}$.

For finite-dimensional complex inner-product spaces $H,K$, vectors $y\in H$ and

$$|x\rangle\langle y|:H\to K,\qquad z\mapsto\langle z,y\rangle_{H,\mathrm{root}}x.$$

$[x][y]^\dagger$, where $[x]$ and $[y]$ are the corresponding coordinate
columns and $M^\dagger:=\overline M^{\mathsf T}$ is the conjugate transpose.
The coordinate assertion is established in
[[thm-qc-dirac-notation-coordinate-identity]].

linear maps $H\to H$ ([[def-linear-map]]).

$$\bigl(\operatorname{Tr}_B(R)\bigr)_{i i'}:=\sum_{j<b}R_{(i,j),(i',j)}.$$

Rows are output coordinates and columns are input coordinates, as in
[[def-coordinate-column-and-matrix-of-a-linear-map]]. If $b=0$, the sum is

factor is contracted; the first factor and its order are retained.

For finite-dimensional complex inner-product spaces $H_A,H_B$, the partial
trace $\operatorname{Tr}_B:\operatorname{End}(H_A\otimes H_B)\to
\operatorname{End}(H_A)$ is the unique linear map satisfying

$$\operatorname{tr}\bigl((\operatorname{Tr}_B R)\circ T\bigr)=\operatorname{tr}\bigl(R\circ(T\otimes I_{H_B})\bigr)\quad\text{for every }R\in\operatorname{End}(H_A\otimes H_B)\text{ and }T\in\operatorname{End}(H_A).$$

Here $I_{H_B}$ is the identity map $y\mapsto y$ on $H_B$; $\operatorname{End}$
is the notation defined in [[def-qc-partial-trace]].

Its coordinate formula is independent of the chosen ordered orthonormal basis
of $H_B$. The assertion includes zero-dimensional factors.

Let $T:V\to W$ be a linear map whose domain $V$ is finite-dimensional over
$F$. Its **nullity** and **rank** are

$$\operatorname{nullity}T:=\dim_F(\ker T),\qquad \operatorname{rank}T:=\dim_F(\operatorname{im}T).$$

Both dimensions are defined. The kernel is a linear subspace of the
finite-dimensional space $V$, so it is finite-dimensional by
[[thm-linear-kernel-image-and-injectivity]] and
[[thm-dimension-of-a-linear-subspace]]. The image is finite-dimensional because
[[lem-kernel-basis-extension-gives-image-basis]] constructs a finite basis of
it from a basis of $V$. Thus rank and nullity are natural numbers, including
when $V$ is the zero space.

Let $V$ be a vector space over a field $F$ ([[def-vector-space]]).

### Finite sums of vectors

By axiom (V1) the triple $(V, +, 0_V)$ is an abelian group ([[def-group]]), hence
in particular a commutative monoid ([[def-semigroup-and-monoid]]). So the finite
products of [[def-monoid-finite-product]] are available in it, and we write them
**additively**: for $n \in \mathbb{N}$ and a finite list $u : n \to V$, that is a
function on the von Neumann natural $n = \{0, \dots, n-1\}$
([[def-natural-numbers]], [[lem-nat-order-is-membership]]),

$$\sum_{i<n} u_i \;:=\; \prod_{i<n} u_i \quad \text{computed in } (V,+,0_V),$$

so that $\sum_{i<0} u_i = 0_V$ and $\sum_{i<\sigma(n)} u_i = \bigl(\sum_{i<n} u_i\bigr) + u_n$,
and the value depends only on $u_0, \dots, u_{n-1}$.

### Linear combinations

A **linear combination in $V$** is a vector of the form

$$\sum_{i<n} \lambda_i v_i$$

where $n \in \mathbb{N}$, $\lambda : n \to F$ is a finite list of scalars and
$v : n \to V$ is a finite list of vectors; the sum is the finite sum just
described, of the list $i \mapsto \lambda_i v_i$. For $S \subseteq V$, a vector
$w \in V$ is a **linear combination of elements of $S$** when there are
$n \in \mathbb{N}$, $\lambda : n \to F$ and $v : n \to S$ with
$w = \sum_{i<n} \lambda_i v_i$.

**The empty case is a real case.** $\mathbb{N}$ contains $0$
([[def-natural-numbers]]), and at $n = 0$ the sum is the empty sum, which is
$0_V$. So $0_V$ is a linear combination of elements of every subset of $V$,
including $S = \varnothing$. The lists are indexed from $0$, so a linear
combination of length $n$ is $\lambda_0 v_0 + \dots + \lambda_{n-1}v_{n-1}$; no
statement here is restricted to $n \ge 1$.

### The span

Let $S \subseteq V$. The set of linear subspaces of $V$ containing $S$ is
nonempty, since $V$ itself is one, so its intersection is a linear subspace of
$V$ by [[lem-intersection-of-linear-subspaces]]. That intersection is the **span
of $S$**,

$$\operatorname{span}(S) \;:=\; \bigcap \{\, W \;:\; W \text{ is a linear subspace of } V \text{ and } S \subseteq W \,\} .$$

It contains $S$, being an intersection of sets each of which contains $S$, and it
is contained in every linear subspace of $V$ that contains $S$. So it is the
**smallest** linear subspace of $V$ containing $S$, and those two properties
determine it uniquely: if $W$ and $W'$ both contain $S$ and are each contained in
every linear subspace containing $S$, then each is contained in the other. This
is what licenses the definite article.

A subset $S \subseteq V$ **spans** $V$, or is a **spanning set** of $V$, when
$\operatorname{span}(S) = V$.

For a linear subspace $W$ ([[def-linear-subspace]]) of an inner product space $V$, using the preceding notion of orthogonality ([[def-orthogonal-vectors-sets-and-orthonormal-bases]]), its **orthogonal complement** is

$$W^\perp:=\{v\in V:\langle v,w\rangle=0\text{ for every }w\in W\}.$$

This is a linear subspace: $0\in W^\perp$, and linearity in the first argument shows that $au+bv\in W^\perp$ whenever $u,v\in W^\perp$ and $a,b$ are scalars. One has $V^\perp=\{0\}$ by positive definiteness and $\{0\}^\perp=V$.

If $W$ is a subspace of a finite-dimensional real or complex inner product space $V$, then

$$V=W\oplus W^\perp.$$

Thus every $v\in V$ has unique vectors $w\in W$ and $z\in W^\perp$ with $v=w+z$.

Let $V$ be a vector space over a field $F$ ([[def-vector-space]]) that is
finite-dimensional with $\dim_F V = n$ ([[def-dimension]]), and let $U$ be a
linear subspace of $V$ ([[def-linear-subspace]]). Then

1. $U$ is finite-dimensional over $F$ and $\dim_F U \le n$;
2. $\dim_F U = n$ **if and only if** $U = V$;
3. **Extension, with no choice principle.** Every linearly independent
   $A_0 \subseteq U$ is contained in a basis of $U$: there is a basis $B$ of $U$
   with $A_0 \subseteq B \subseteq U$. Claim 1 is the case $A_0 = \varnothing$.
   Since $V$ is itself a linear subspace of $V$ ([[def-linear-subspace]]), claim 3
   applies with $V$ in place of $U$, and hence to **any** finite-dimensional
   vector space over $F$ in place of the pair $(V, U)$.

**Nothing above uses a choice principle**, and claim 3 in particular is the
finite-dimensional substitute for the Zorn-based extension theorem stated earlier
on this page. In finite dimension the extension terminates on its own, because
[[cor-independent-set-is-no-larger-than-a-finite-spanning-set]] bounds the size
of an independent set and [[thm-well-ordering-principle]] then supplies a largest
one; no selection is made anywhere.

**Finiteness is essential in claim 2.** Without it the equality case fails: the
companion page exhibits a
proper linear subspace of an infinite-dimensional space whose basis is
equinumerous with a basis of the whole space.
Every finite-dimensional real or complex inner product space has an orthonormal basis. In dimension zero, this is the empty basis.

Let $V$ be a vector space over a field $F$ ([[def-vector-space]]).

$V$ is **finite-dimensional over $F$** when it has a **finite** basis
([[def-linear-basis]], [[def-countable]]): some basis $B$ of $V$ satisfies
$B \approx n$ for some $n \in \mathbb{N}$ ([[def-equinumerous]]).

For such a $V$, the **dimension of $V$ over $F$**, written $\dim_F V$, is that
$n$:

$$\dim_F V \;:=\; \text{the unique } n \in \mathbb{N} \text{ such that } V \text{ has a basis } B \text{ with } B \approx n .$$

**This is well defined.** Existence of such an $n$ is the hypothesis, together
with the fact that a finite set is equinumerous with exactly one natural number
([[lem-pigeonhole]], claim 3). Uniqueness is
[[thm-any-two-finite-bases-have-the-same-size]]: two bases of $V$ with $n$ and
with $m$ elements force $n = m$. That theorem is therefore a **prerequisite** of
this definition, not a later justification of it, and it is listed in `deps`.

$V$ is **infinite-dimensional over $F$** when it is not finite-dimensional over
$F$, that is, when $V$ has **no** finite basis. No number is attached to such a
space here: the symbol $\dim_F V$ is defined only in the finite-dimensional case,
and the expression $\dim_F V = \infty$ is not used.

**The zero space.** $\varnothing$ is a basis of $\{0_V\}$
([[def-linear-basis]]) and $\varnothing \approx 0$, so $\{0_V\}$ is
finite-dimensional with $\dim_F \{0_V\} = 0$. Conversely a space of dimension $0$
has a basis $B \approx 0$, that is $B = \varnothing$, and then
$V = \operatorname{span}(\varnothing) = \{0_V\}$
([[def-linear-combination-and-span]]).
Every finite orthogonal list of nonzero vectors in an inner product space is linearly independent. The empty list is included.

Let $V$ be a vector space over a field $F$ ([[def-vector-space]]) and suppose
$V$ has a spanning subset $S$ ([[def-linear-combination-and-span]]) with
$S \approx n$ for some $n \in \mathbb{N}$ ([[def-equinumerous]]). Then:

1. every linearly independent subset $L \subseteq V$
   ([[def-linear-independence]]) is finite ([[def-countable]]), and the unique
   $m \in \mathbb{N}$ with $L \approx m$ satisfies $m \le n$;
2. no linearly independent subset of $V$ is equinumerous with $\mathbb{N}$.

Let $F$ be a field ([[def-field]]), let $n \in \mathbb{N}$ and let $F^{n}$ be the
function space on the von Neumann natural $n = \{0, \dots, n-1\}$, with the
pointwise operations ([[def-function-space]], [[def-natural-numbers]],
[[lem-nat-order-is-membership]]). For $i < n$ define the **standard unit vector**
$e_i \in F^{n}$ by

$$e_i(i) = 1_F, \qquad e_i(j) = 0_F \ \text{ for } j < n \text{ with } j \ne i .$$

Then:

1. **Finite sums in a function space are pointwise.** For every set $X$, every
   $p \in \mathbb{N}$, every list $u : p \to F^{X}$ and every $j \in X$,
   $$\Bigl(\sum_{k<p} u_k\Bigr)(j) \;=\; \sum_{k<p} u_k(j),$$
   the right-hand sum being taken in $(F,+,0_F)$. (Stated here for an arbitrary
   $X$ because the companion page needs it at $X = \mathbb{N}$.)
2. $e : n \to F^{n}$ is an ordered basis of $F^{n}$ ([[def-linear-basis]]); in
   particular $e$ is injective and its image $e[n] = \{\, e_i : i < n \,\}$ is a
   basis of $F^{n}$ with $e[n] \approx n$ ([[def-equinumerous]]);
3. for every $\lambda : n \to F$ and every $j < n$,
   $\bigl(\sum_{i<n}\lambda_i e_i\bigr)(j) = \lambda_j$; equivalently the
   coordinate list of $x \in F^{n}$ with respect to the ordered basis $e$
   ([[thm-unique-coordinates-with-respect-to-an-ordered-basis]]) is
   $i \mapsto x(i)$;
4. $F^{n}$ is finite-dimensional over $F$ with $\dim_F F^{n} = n$
   ([[def-dimension]]);
5. at $n = 0$ this reads: $F^{0}$ has exactly one element, the empty function,
   so $F^{0}$ is the zero space, the empty list is its ordered basis,
   $\varnothing$ is its basis and $\dim_F F^{0} = 0$.

Every index runs from $0$, so the coordinates of an element of $F^{n}$ are
$x_0, \dots, x_{n-1}$ and no statement above is restricted to $n \ge 1$.

For $x,y\in\mathbb R^n$ and $z,w\in\mathbb C^n$, the formulas

$$\langle x,y\rangle_{\mathbb R^n}=\sum_{k<n}x_ky_k,\qquad \langle z,w\rangle_{\mathbb C^n}=\sum_{k<n}z_k\overline{w_k}$$

define inner products, linear in the first argument. At $n=0$, the unique pairing on the zero space is an inner product.

An **ordered tensor register** consists of a finite ordered list of
finite-dimensional complex inner-product spaces $H_0,\ldots,H_{n-1}$, each
equipped with a specified ordered orthonormal basis. Its space is
$H_0\otimes\cdots\otimes H_{n-1}$, with factors retained in the displayed
order. The product basis is ordered lexicographically by its tuple of factor
indices. The empty tensor product is $\mathbb C$ with basis $\{1\}$. A
zero-dimensional factor is allowed in this mathematical construction and makes
the tensor space zero; it is not a register under
[[def-qc-register-and-computational-basis]].

The inner product is linear in the first argument and conjugate-linear in the
second, and on elementary tensors it is

$$\left\langle\bigotimes_{k<n}x_k,\bigotimes_{k<n}y_k\right\rangle_{\otimes}:=\prod_{k<n}\langle x_k,y_k\rangle_{{\rm root},k}.$$ 

For the empty tensor, the right side is the empty product $1$, giving the
standard inner product on $\mathbb C$.

For a permutation $\sigma$ of the $n$ factor positions, the **wire permutation**
$P_\sigma$ maps the product basis vector indexed by
$(i_0,\ldots,i_{n-1})$ to the product basis vector whose output factor order is
$(\sigma(0),\ldots,\sigma(n-1))$. It is extended linearly; for $n=0$ it is the
identity on $\mathbb C$. The extension is a linear map in the sense of
[[def-linear-map]].

For a complex vector space $H$, write $\operatorname{End}(H)$ for the set of
linear maps $H\to H$ ([[def-linear-map]]).

Let $H_A,H_B$ be finite-dimensional complex inner-product spaces with fixed
ordered orthonormal bases $(e_i)_{i<a}$ and $(f_j)_{j<b}$, respectively. The
ordered product basis of $H_A\otimes H_B$ has the $A$ index first. For
$R\in\operatorname{End}(H_A\otimes H_B)$ define
$\operatorname{Tr}_B(R)\in\operatorname{End}(H_A)$ by

$$\bigl(\operatorname{Tr}_B(R)\bigr)_{i i'}:=\sum_{j<b}R_{(i,j),(i',j)}.$$

Rows are output coordinates and columns are input coordinates, as in
[[def-coordinate-column-and-matrix-of-a-linear-map]]. If $b=0$, the sum is
empty and equals $0$. The notation $\operatorname{Tr}_B$ means that the second
factor is contracted; the first factor and its order are retained.

All complex inner products in this track use the root convention: they are
linear in the first argument and conjugate-linear in the second
([[def-real-and-complex-inner-product-space]]). For vectors $x,y$ in the same
space, define the Dirac pairing by

$$\langle x|y\rangle_D:=\langle y,x\rangle_{\mathrm{root}}.$$

The ket $|x\rangle$ denotes the vector $x$. The bra $\langle x|$ denotes the
linear functional $z\mapsto\langle z,x\rangle_{\mathrm{root}}$.

For finite-dimensional complex inner-product spaces $H,K$, vectors $y\in H$ and
$x\in K$, define the rank-one linear map

$$|x\rangle\langle y|:H\to K,\qquad z\mapsto\langle z,y\rangle_{H,\mathrm{root}}x.$$

Given ordered orthonormal bases of $H$ and $K$, its coordinate matrix is
$[x][y]^\dagger$, where $[x]$ and $[y]$ are the corresponding coordinate
columns and $M^\dagger:=\overline M^{\mathsf T}$ is the conjugate transpose.
The coordinate assertion is established in
[[thm-qc-dirac-notation-coordinate-identity]].

For nonzero finite-dimensional complex-inner-product $H$, the map sending a ray $[u]$ to the rank-one projector $P_u=|u\rangle\langle u|$ of any unit representative is well-defined and bijective onto the rank-one orthogonal projections on $H$. Each $P_u$ is non-negative and has trace one.

Let $H$ be a nonzero finite-dimensional complex inner-product space, with the root library's convention that the inner product is linear in its first argument. A **density operator** on $H$ is a non-negative endomorphism $\rho:H\to H$ with $\operatorname{tr}(\rho)=1$; non-negative and trace have the meanings of [[def-non-negative-and-positive-operator]] and [[def-trace-of-an-endomorphism]]. The zero-dimensional space is excluded: its only endomorphism has trace $0$.

Here $\ker\rho=\{x\in H:\rho x=0\}$, using the kernel of a linear map from [[def-kernel-and-image-of-a-linear-map]]. The **support** of $\rho$ is the orthogonal complement of its kernel in the root convention:

$$\operatorname{supp}(\rho):=\{x\in H: \langle x,y\rangle=0\text{ for every }y\in\ker\rho\}.$$

For a subspace $S\subseteq H$, $\rho$ is **faithful on $S$** when $\operatorname{supp}(\rho)=S$ and the restriction $\rho|_S:S\to S$ is positive definite in the sense of [[def-non-negative-and-positive-operator]]. This restriction is an endomorphism: if $x\in S$ and $y\in\ker\rho$, self-adjointness gives $\langle\rho x,y\rangle=\langle x,\rho y\rangle=0$, so $\rho x\in(\ker\rho)^\perp=S$.

Let $H$ be a nonzero finite-dimensional complex-inner-product space. A **finite ensemble of density operators** on $H$ is a positive integer $n$, weights $p_1,\ldots,p_n\ge0$ with $\sum_{a=1}^np_a=1$, and density operators $\rho_1,\ldots,\rho_n$ on $H$. Its **barycenter** is $\bar\rho=\sum_{a=1}^np_a\rho_a$. A zero-weight component still names a density operator but contributes zero to the barycenter.

Let $K$ be any finite-dimensional complex-inner-product space. A **purification** of a density operator $\rho$ on $H$ is a unit vector $\Psi\in H\otimes K$ such that

$$\operatorname{Tr}_K(|\Psi\rangle\langle\Psi|)=\rho.$$

The tensor factors are ordered $H$ then $K$. Tensor products, outer products and partial trace have the conventions of [[def-qc-tensor-register-and-permutation]], [[def-qc-dirac-notation-conversion]] and [[def-qc-partial-trace]]. The auxiliary space may be any finite dimension that supports such a unit vector.

Then:

1. **Finite sums in a function space are pointwise.** For every set $X$, every

4. $F^{n}$ is finite-dimensional over $F$ with $\dim_F F^{n} = n$
   ([[def-dimension]]);
5. at $n = 0$ this reads: $F^{0}$ has exactly one element, the empty function,
   so $F^{0}$ is the zero space, the empty list is its ordered basis,
   $\varnothing$ is its basis and $\dim_F F^{0} = 0$.

Every index runs from $0$, so the coordinates of an element of $F^{n}$ are

Every nonzero finite-dimensional complex inner-product space $H$ admits a density operator; specifically, if $d=\dim_{\mathbb C}H$, then $I_H/d$ is a density operator on $H$.

derivations.claim: By [F1]–[F2], $e_0,e_1$ are an ordered orthonormal basis. Taking $u_j=e_j$ and $v_j=e_j$ for $j=0,1$, the displayed expression for $\Psi$ is a finite sum with positive coefficients $s_0=s_1=1/\sqrt2$ and orthonormal families in both factors. The product basis from [F3] is orthonormal, so $\|\Psi\|^2=\frac12(1+1)=1$. Hence this expression is a Schmidt form by the finite-sum definition in the statement.

Expanding the outer product using [F5] gives $|\Psi\rangle\langle\Psi|=\frac12(|e_0e_0\rangle\langle e_0e_0|+|e_0e_0\rangle\langle e_1e_1|+|e_1e_1\rangle\langle e_0e_0|+|e_1e_1\rangle\langle e_1e_1|)$. Contracting the second factor by [F4] kills the cross terms and leaves $\frac12(|e_0\rangle\langle e_0|+|e_1\rangle\langle e_1|)=I_2/2$.

The factor permutation in [F3] sends $e_0\otimes e_0$ and $e_1\otimes e_1$ to themselves, so the reordered vector has the same expression as $\Psi$. Apply [F4] to trace its second factor, now the original $H$ factor; the same contraction as in step 1.2 gives $\frac12(|e_0\rangle\langle e_0|+|e_1\rangle\langle e_1|)=I_2/2$ on the original $K$.

Set $|+\rangle=(e_0+e_1)/\sqrt2$ and $|-\rangle=(e_0-e_1)/\sqrt2$, and write $P_v=|v\rangle\langle v|$ for $v=e_0,e_1,+,-$. These vectors are unit by [F1]–[F2], so [F6] makes their projectors density operators. By [F7], the pairs $(\frac12,P_{e_0}), (\frac12,P_{e_1})$ and $(\frac12,P_+),(\frac12,P_-)$ are finite ensembles. Expanding the outer products with [F5] gives $P_++P_-=P_{e_0}+P_{e_1}$. Since $(e_0,e_1)$ is an orthonormal basis by [F1]–[F2], each $z\in\mathbb C^2$ satisfies $z=\langle z,e_0\rangle e_0+\langle z,e_1\rangle e_1$, so $P_{e_0}+P_{e_1}=I_2$. Both ensemble barycenters are therefore $I_2/2$, which is a density operator by [F8]. The ensembles are distinct because $P_{e_0}$ and $P_+$ have different one-dimensional ranges. Thus the same density operator has two ensemble descriptions.
